questions.q: Why can an implicit conversion silently defeat an index seek even with no function visibly wrapping the column?
options: Comparing operands of different data types can force SQL Server to convert the indexed column's value per row, based on data type precedence rules
Implicit conversions only ever happen at the application layer, never inside SQL Server
SQL Server refuses to execute any query with mismatched data types
Implicit conversions always convert the literal, never the column
questions.explain: Depending on precedence rules, the conversion can land on the column side, forcing it to be evaluated per row and making the predicate non-sargable with no visible function.

It permanently disables locking for the entire database
It guarantees the fastest possible execution plan for any query
It automatically commits any open transaction on the table
questions.explain: NOLOCK is a correctness tradeoff, not a universal speed switch — it can return uncommitted data that gets rolled back, or duplicate/skip rows during concurrent modification.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when is NOLOCK an acceptable choice?
options: Occasionally, for something like a rough dashboard count where 'close enough' is genuinely acceptable — not as a reflexive fix for blocking that should be properly diagnosed
Always, on every query, as a default performance optimization
Only on financial transaction tables
Only when the table has no indexes at all
questions.explain: The lesson frames NOLOCK as a narrow, occasional tradeoff — not a general performance switch, and not a substitute for properly diagnosing blocking.

questions.q: Why does calling a scalar UDF from a WHERE clause act like a hidden cursor, per this lesson?
options: Prior to SQL Server 2019's inlining improvements, a scalar UDF called in a WHERE clause typically executes once per candidate row, mirroring row-by-row overhead
Scalar UDFs can only be called from inside a cursor loop
Scalar UDFs always return an entire table rather than a single value
SQL Server rewrites every scalar UDF call into a CURSOR internally by design, with no performance difference
questions.explain: A scalar UDF executed once per row against every candidate row reproduces the same row-by-row overhead Lesson 19 identified in cursors, just disguised as a function call.

questions.q: What is the correct fix for `WHERE OrderNumber = 100245` when OrderNumber is an nvarchar(20) column?
options: WHERE OrderNumber = '100245' — matching the literal's type to the column's actual type
Add WITH (NOLOCK) to the query
Wrap OrderNumber in a scalar UDF
Convert OrderNumber to an int column with no other changes
questions.explain: Matching the literal's data type to the column avoids forcing an implicit conversion on the indexed column, keeping the predicate sargable.
